title: Where Snap City occurs
summary: First of a three-part injury-prevention series: NH argues injuries are caused by mistakes, not fate, and that 99% happen at the end of the negative where the lift reverses and form breaks down under load. Solutions are controlled negatives, owning technique from first to last rep, and trimming the riskiest end of the range of motion.
claims: Injuries are the result of cyclical adaptation failure, meaning you are doing something wrong; the fatalistic view that injuries just happen is garbage
An injury is a gap in tonnage where you cannot train and your mental health sinks, so understanding prevention is essential
Injury occurs where the body is weakest, muscularly and structurally; when muscles cannot hold a position the structure shifts into a different stance and overloads other tissues
Hips shooting up in a deadlift means hamstrings, glutes and core cannot hold position, so the lower back takes over
It is the dynamic change of position under load that causes injury: pulling with a rounded back from start to finish is less risky than a neutral spine that rounds under the bar
Elbow flare on an unloaded bench motion is harmless; the same pattern under heavy load is what snaps
Bodybuilders must own technique from rep one to the last rep; form breakdown may be acceptable in strength competition but not for people training for size
99% of injuries occur at the end of the negative (bottom of squat or bench, start of deadlift); almost nobody gets hurt at lockout
A properly done deadlift is very safe because it starts with the positive, letting you see form breakdown coming and abort the pull
Lifts that open with the negative tempt you to grind because you are much stronger eccentrically; many can lower weights they could never press back up
The good morning is the riskiest lift for Snap City: a failed positive forces you back down through the range with fatigued muscles and tendons
The bottom of the negative carries the most muscular and mechanical stress, making it both the best part for hypertrophy and the riskiest
Emphasize slower, controlled negatives and do not dive-bomb, because negative technique dictates positive technique
On curls, avoid fully extending the arm at the bottom, since past a point you only stretch the tendon
Do not cut range short to avoid the bottom 'red zone' entirely, but avoid its deepest part: e.g. avoid butt wink in the squat because it promotes spinal rounding
On bench, pausing slightly shy of the chest to avoid elbow flaring or shoulder rotation costs little hypertrophy and saves shoulders
If you cannot pull from the floor safely, use sumo or block pulls to raise the danger zone
Lifting slightly less weight with a slightly shorter range for years beats full-range work that gets you injured every three to four months
exercises: highest risk of failing in a compromised position
pause slightly shy of chest if shoulders flare/rotate
alternative if conventional from floor is unsafe
abort the pull if back rounds
starts with the positive, safe when done properly
